task: Fix the configuration injection vulnerability after user input was used directly in config keys.

candidate_memories.content: Security scan found that user-supplied names can inject arbitrary config keys through the account settings endpoint.
The account settings endpoint must whitelist permitted config key names before accepting user input.
The vulnerability was introduced when the config key format was made dynamic for customization flexibility.
The injection risk is limited to authenticated users with account settings access; unauthenticated requests are unaffected.
Session 4 note: the security team flagged a config key injection pattern in their automated SAST scan results.
The account settings API uses a generic key-value config store for user-configurable settings.
Session 5 note: the security team added a SAST scanner to the CI pipeline.
Old practice: config keys were hardcoded enum values before the dynamic key format was introduced.
The config store uses a prefix to namespace user-configurable keys from system keys.
Session 10 note: the security team completed a penetration test and found no SQL injection vulnerabilities.
Old config guide: the dynamic key format was added to support plugin-based customization.
User-supplied config keys must be validated against an allowlist before being stored or processed.
Session 7 note: the platform team added input sanitization for all user-facing form fields.
The config store enforces a maximum key length of 64 characters for all stored keys.
A security review in session 3 found no injection vulnerabilities in the original hardcoded key design.
The account settings endpoint requires the account:settings:write scope for all write operations.
Dynamic configuration systems must use strict input validation to prevent injection attacks.
Session 12 note: the security team added a runtime WAF rule to detect config injection patterns.
Old endpoint guide: the config key format was validated only by length before the dynamic format was added.
User-configurable settings are scoped to the account; they cannot affect system-level configuration.
